title: The Lost Photograph
passage:
While helping clean his aunt's house, Koji found a small black-and-white photograph under a drawer. It showed six people standing in front of a wooden building. Nobody in the picture looked familiar to him, and there was no name on the front. Koji almost placed it in a box of old paper, but his aunt asked him to keep it until they knew what it was.

They looked at the back and found a date written in pencil: 1968. There was also one word, ‘Hoshikawa,’ which was the name of a nearby district. Koji's aunt called his grandmother. She could not identify everyone, but she recognized the wooden building as an old community hall that had been pulled down before Koji was born. She suggested asking Mr. Abe, a neighbor who had lived in the area since childhood.

Mr. Abe studied the photograph carefully. After a minute, he smiled. Two of the people were his older brothers. The group had been volunteers who organized a summer festival. The wooden hall was where they stored drums and lanterns. Mr. Abe explained that the festival stopped for several years after the hall closed, but younger residents later started it again in a different park. He had not seen a picture of the old hall for a long time.

Koji scanned the photograph and made a digital copy. His aunt gave the original to Mr. Abe because his family appeared in it. With permission, Koji also sent the scan to the local community center. A staff member added it to a small online collection of neighborhood history, along with the date and information Mr. Abe had provided.

Koji was surprised by how much information had come from one photograph with almost no writing on it. The image itself had not explained the story. The story appeared only when several people shared what they knew. He realized that old objects can be like unfinished questions. A date, a place name, a memory, and a conversation can connect them to a larger history.
translation:
叔母の家の片付けを手伝っていたコウジは、引き出しの下から小さな白黒写真を見つけました。木造の建物の前に六人が立っていますが、知っている顔はなく、表に名前もありません。古紙の箱へ入れようとすると、叔母は正体が分かるまで取っておこうと言いました。

裏を見ると、鉛筆で『1968』と書かれ、『星川』という近くの地区名もありました。叔母が祖母へ電話すると、全員の顔は分からないものの、建物はコウジが生まれる前に取り壊された昔の公民館だと分かりました。さらに、子どもの頃から地域に住む阿部さんへ聞いてみることになりました。

阿部さんは写真をじっと見てから笑顔になりました。写っている二人は彼の兄たちで、夏祭りを運営していたボランティアの仲間でした。木造の会館には太鼓や提灯を保管していたそうです。会館が閉じた後、祭りは数年間中止されましたが、若い住民が別の公園で再開したことも教えてくれました。

コウジは写真をスキャンしてデジタル化しました。叔母は原本を阿部さんへ渡し、許可を得てスキャン画像を地域センターにも送りました。職員は、阿部さんから聞いた日付や情報とともに、地域史の小さなオンライン資料へ加えました。

ほとんど文字のない一枚の写真から、これほど多くの情報が出てきたことにコウジは驚きました。写真そのものが物語を語ったわけではありません。複数の人が知っていることを持ち寄った時に物語が現れたのです。古い物は未完成の問いのようなものかもしれません。日付、地名、記憶、会話が結びつくことで、より大きな歴史へつながるのです。
